newsitem.title: USA: ITALY'S GIACOMO LEONE WINS NEW YORK MARATHON. [corrected 23:13 gmt]
newsitem.headline: ITALY'S GIACOMO LEONE WINS NEW YORK MARATHON. [corrected 23:13 gmt]

text.p: Giacomo Leone of Italy surprised a powerful contingent of African runners on Sunday, making a late move to win the New York City Marathon.
Leone, 25, broke clear in the 25th mile, moving strongly up a hill after entering Central Park. He never was challenged over the final mile, handily beating Turbo Tummo of Ethiopia.
"The finish was very hard during the last five miles, but I did very well," said Leone, who suffered a stress fracture early in the year and didn't qualify for the Italian Olympic team.

Leone's winning time was 2 hours, 9 minutes, 54 seconds, well off the course record of 2:08:01 set by Juma Ikangaa of Tanzania in 1989. Leone ran a 2:09:34 when he finished second in Venice, Italy, in October 1995, but the time isn't official because the course was found to be 80 yards (metres) short.
Kenyan runners took three of the next four places, with Joseph Kamau third, John Kagwe fourth and Cosmas Ndeti sixth. Mexican Andres Espinosa was fifth.
There was also a surprise in the women's event as Anuta Catuna (corrects spelling of surname) of Romania, who was 44th in the Atlanta Olympics, came on strong to win in 2:28:18.
Franca Fiacconi gave Italy another proud moment when she finished second in 2:28:42 and Joyce Chepchumba of Kenya was third.

Another Kenyan, two-time defending champion Tegla Loroupe, set the early pace but faded badly to finish seventh. After crossing the finish line, Loroupe was taken by stretcher to the medical tent in Central Park. She was said to be suffering from stomach cramps.
The men ran the first mile in a relatively slow 4:52, but the pace soon quickened.

Hamid Oubadris of France, who is not an elite runner, was the early pacesetter. Oubadris, third in a marathon in Cannes, France, in June, led through 11 miles before giving way to a Kenyan, Lazarus Nyakeraka.
Espinosa, who was not among the lead pack during the first half, moved in front in the 16th mile, just a few steps in front of William Musyoki of Kenya.
By the 19th mile Kamau was leading with Espinosa second and Tummo third. Nearing the park Espinosa dropped back to fourth as Leone, Tummo and Ndeti maintained close contact.

Loroupe got off to an impressive start and her time of 48:53 for nine miles was faster than the course record of 48:57. She remained in front through 20 miles before yielding to her training partner, Chepchumba.
Catuna, in third place at the time, remained close until making her late move.
The winners each earned $30,000 and a new car.
